utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Registrar, please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning to everyone in the courtroom. This is case number IT-04-74-T, the Prosecutor versus Prlic et al. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Today is Wednesday, June 20th. I'd like to say good morning to the witness, to the Prosecutor, and to the Defence counsel, and good morning to the accused as well. I know that Mr. Coric is not feeling well. I hope he will be back with us very soon, and I understand that Mr. Sahota wanted to take the floor so I'm going to give him the floor right now.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAHOTA
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would like to make a short oral application on behalf of all the Defence teams for an extension of the time limits to reply to two new motions that were filed recently on the -- dated the 12th of June, 2007. Both relate to evidence to be adduced relevant to the Ljubuski municipality. Both motions relate to a substantial volume of material which has been served in support. The first motion, which is a motion brought under Rule 92 bis, has around 300 pages of supporting material. The second motion, which is a motion to adduce documentary evidence, has in the region -- or in excess of, I understand, 1.500 pages of material. The Defence are at the moment endeavouring to see whether it is possible to file a joint response to both motions. The Defence teams are also currently engaged in drafting responses to other substantial motions that were recently filed by the Prosecution, including a motion pertaining to 47 separate UN documents for which the Trial Chamber has kindly granted an extension of the deadline for a reply to be filed until the end of this month. Mr. President, I don't think there's any prejudice to any party in our application which is for an extension of the deadline for a response to be filed until the 12th of July, 2007.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: The Prosecution has no objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Scott.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: No objections, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Fine. The Chamber, after having considered the matter, having heard the application and the comments made by the Prosecution, will grant you an extension of time until the 12th of July, 2007. We'll now continue with the cross-examination of the witness. I was told that you've used one hour and five minutes, Mr. Karnavas. Who gave you the additional 55 minutes?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I received 30 minutes, I believe, from Mr. Coric, 30 minutes from Mr. Pusic, and there may be a possibility that some additional time may be granted to me by one of the other teams. May I proceed?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please proceed, because Mr. Coric has given you 30 minutes and Mr. Pusic as well. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Very well. And with that, since you've raised the issue of time, Your Honour, let me just say that I don't have sufficient time, even with the time that's being allotted to me. I just want to make sure that the record is there, especially with 120 paragraphs of a statement that's coming in by the Prosecution; and in light of the Prosecution's remarks yesterday, if anything goes uncontroverted through this witness, then the Trial Chamber should accept it as fact. And so based on that, I just want to make sure the record is clear, that if these are the rules of evidence, if this is how the burden of proof is to be applied in this courtroom, certainly, we can never get a fair trial. With that in mind and with the record having been made, I will proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, madam. I'd like to turn to document 3708. That is Prosecution document.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Perhaps the usher would be so kind as to give the witness the binder.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: This was a document that an opportunity to see --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: The Prosecutor's binder. I don't mean to be snapping, but if this time is going to be counted against me.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: 3708. This was a letter dated the 26th of July, 1993, and it was visited upon you yesterday by Mr. -- or the day before by the Prosecutor. This is from Mr. Rebic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: 3708. Okay. Funny how things go. Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, do you recall seeing this letter? We talked about it yesterday. Madam, there's no need to study it. It was shown to you by the Prosecution. You commented on it. Now, you either recognise it or you don't recognise it. Do you recognise the document, a document shown to you by the Prosecution, a document that the Prosecution went over with you, a document that you and your colleague, Ms. Turkovic, turned over to the Prosecution. Do you recognise it, yes or no?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Excuse me, Your Honour. There is no point to this. The witness has -- it's fair for the witness to look at a document before answering a question. It's been overnight. Come on. Let's not start the day this way.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I don't have enough time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Do you recognise the document, madam, now that you put on your reading glasses? Do you recognise the document?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: She understands English.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have checked this, and I do know the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Now, in a second paragraph, it says here that "Croatia has till today accepted 600.000 refugees from Bosnia and Herzegovina of which 277.000 are still in Croatia." Was that the case to your knowledge; that is, that Croatia had until that period of time received 600.000 refugees from Bosnia and almost half of them were still in Croatia at that point in time? Was that a fact?

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: It corresponds to the figures that were published at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, if we turn over the next page, you were read a portion yesterday and then we saw another document from the ambassador, where Mr. Rebic is noting his surprise that the ambassador had not visited the 6.138 expelled Croats from the Lasva Valley. We're not going to -- I just want to point that out. I'm going to bring this up in a later document, but do you recall being asked questions about this from the Prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Very well. I'll just move on. Now, in the latter part of this page, if we go to the second to last paragraph, it says: "In accordance with the current politics, we have not differentiated between the Croats and Muslims as you have. In hotels we have Muslims, just as in refugee centres we have Croats. Proof Spansko is one suburb of Muslim refugees with Croats, in another just a little further are displaced Vukovar people." Do you see that? Do you accept that or not, that representation made by Mr. Rebic?

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't agree with this.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. And if we turn to the next page, we can look at the --

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I apologise, but I can't follow you that quickly. I've just now located the paragraph, and I can say that I agree with what Mr. Rebic observes, that in the hotels there were both Muslims, as there were Croats in refugee centres. That is something that I agree with.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Very well. Thank you for that clarification. Now, if you turn to the next page, the last page, starting with the paragraph where it says -- where it begins "Furthermore," Mr. Rebic says: "Furthermore, I would like to warn you that all refugee centres and hotels are open and free, and so all refugees have full freedom of movement and visiting, as was proved by your visit in contacts with refugees." Now, is it my understanding that you take exception with that; in other words, that the centres were not -- were not open?

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't understand the question. It says here or Dr. Rebic here says that they're open.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. And do you disagree with that?

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could you be more specific in your question?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Let me just read -- let me just read the portion and then see if you agree or disagree: "Furthermore, I would like to warn you that all refugee centres and hotels are open and free, and so all refugees have full freedom of movement and visiting, as well -- as was proved by your visit and contacts with refugees. And that is not the case in other countries. We know that well. We always had to have permission when we visited refugee camps in neighbouring countries where accommodated were Croatian citizens." Now, do you agree with that or not? There's two parts.

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I agree fully with the first part. As to the second part, I don't have an opinion because I don't have the necessary information.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Very well. Now, the next document, again, this was shown to you by the Prosecution and this is 3765. 3765. This was a letter by Ms. Turkovic.

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: The document isn't here.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: There's another binder, and I'm not sure that this was the binder that was given to the witness yesterday by the Prosecutor. The big binder. If that's the Prosecution's binder, then when I make reference to a Prosecution document, Mr. Usher, could you kindly assist the witness in giving her that binder because the documents would be in that binder, because they're a Prosecution exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PRANDLER
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Mr. Karnavas, to interrupt you. I really would like to ask you and to request you not to create a kind of nervous atmosphere here in the courtroom. We have to be in a way more tolerant to each other, and I believe the witness is trying to cooperate and also the usher, and really I think that we don't need to have a kind of showdown. Let us listen to each other. I know that you are complaining. You have been complaining a number times that you not have enough time, but anyway, now you have your one hour more, and let us use it well, but don't try to be intolerant to the witness. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Your Honour, if the time that it takes to show a document to a witness is not counted against me I can wait five minutes. But if I have to show five documents and it takes three minutes for each document, that's 30 minutes from my time. It's not that I'm complaining. It is that this Trial Chamber is not granting me the time that I need to represent my client. I've made that clear. It is not a complaint. It is a fact. You're allowing 120 paragraphs of a statement to come in, and you're granting us collectively six hours, one hour each. It's not fair but I have to rush, and I don't mean to be rude.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: If you look at this document, ma'am, this was a letter shown to you, again, it was by Ms. Turkovic, dated 28 July 1993. Do you see that? You've seen this, have you not?

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: The document is before me and, yes, I have seen it before.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. And this is the document where the ambassador claims to have visited the Croat -- the Croat refugees; correct? If you look at the bottom, this was shown to you by the Prosecutor; and, in fact, you testified that both the ambassador and you had gone to see the Croats, and, again, the date is 28 July 1993.

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I still maintain that I visited the Croats, and I also claim that the ambassador did the same.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Now, again, I point the date out, 28 July 1993, because the next document, 4150, this is a Prosecution document, 4150, again, this was shown to you yesterday or the day before by the Prosecutor, and this is dated 13th of August, 1993. And, in fact, when you find it, you will see that this is a document that you yourself generated and in fact signed. If you just go to the back -- the last page, you'll see your name there as the attache for refugees. Do you see this document?

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have the document in front of me.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Very well. And you recognise the document?

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do recognise it, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And this is a document that you prepared?

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Precisely.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Now, if we go to the page where, if you look at the very top part you see some numbers, these are ERN numbers. It's 0218-8969, 0218-8969. It would be the last page on B/C/S, I'm told. And it would be the second last page in English for those of us following the English. And, again, I point the date on the very first page is 13th of August. If we look at the second to last paragraph, the second to last paragraph, and let me read it; it's short. And this is a letter that you're drafting and you're sending to the government of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, to the Ministry of Foreign Affairs, and here's what you state: "About the refugees of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina- Croats, sadly, we have no information at all, as we do not receive the information about them nor do we receive any other information from the office of displaced and refugees, and they themselves are not contacting the embassy. We hope that you will understand that due to these kinds of difficulties, we are unable to provide a better quality analysis of the problematic of the refugees from the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina- Croats." Now, it seems to me somebody is providing false information. Either you're providing false information to the government, your own government, about those Croats, or Ms. Turkovic is providing false information when she states that she visited, she visited these Croats refugees from Bosnia-Herzegovina, because again I point to the dates. Her letter in response to the previous letter is 28 July 1993, and here you are two weeks later, two weeks later you're saying, "We don't know anything about Croats." Now, this is in your report. You generated it. You have acknowledged that this is your report. Do you have any explanation to why you're informing your own government from Croatia that you know nothing about Croat refugees?

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: May I be allowed to answer?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'd just like to ask you to read this out very precisely what I'm informing the government about, and that is that I do not have information about the problems that possibly Croat refugees have at that point in time, because they didn't come and contact me, they didn't phone me up, and they are dealing with the conditions under which they're living without any assistance. And that is what it says here. What I'm doing is I'm informing them. I'm telling them that I can't deal with the problem of Croat refugees because I just don't have the necessary information about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Excuse me. If you go to your report, and this is why I would need like two days to cross-examine you, but if you were to go to your report, you indicated that one of your functions was to write reports. You know, paragraph 14 of your own statement: "While I was -- while I was at that position, I would produce reports whenever they were needed." Now, it would seem to me, madam, that had you visited these Croats, as you have represented, and had Ms. Turkovic visited these Croats, as she had been representing, certainly, you would have some evidence or some facts or some information to pass on to the authorities as opposed to telling them, as you do in this particular document, and these are your words, not mine, where you say: "We have no information at all, as we do not receive the information about them, nor do we receive any other information from the office of displaced -- of displaced and refugees." And you go on so on and so forth. So if you had visited them, if Turkovic had visited them and had spoken to them and had seen their conditions and was able to talk to them, there would have been some information to pass on to the authorities, other than to say to them, We know nothing about the Croats of Bosnia-Herzegovina, as you represent being the attache, and you're representing this to your own government back in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Would you please look at my report, the report in which I informed my government in Sarajevo about the visit to the Croats, the Bosnian Croats who were put up in Pinete.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I'm going to move on madam because I've shown you the dates. This are two weeks after Ms. Turkovic claimed to have seen these refugees. And what you're -- you're mixing apples and oranges, with all due respect, but we'll move on. Let's look at 1D 01583. It's very quickly and it goes back to what Mr. Rebic was saying and what you are claiming. Have you ever -- it's in my documents. It's a Defence document. 1D 01583. And we see it's dated March 11, 1993. It's called "Asyl Times." Are you familiar with this document?

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've never seen this document before. This is the first time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Were there any Muslim refugees in Denmark?

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: To the best of my knowledge, there were refugees from BH in Denmark.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Right. Because if we look at page 4, in the English version at least, your name is even mentioned in it, that they were able to obtain elementary school plans and curricula from the -- your embassy, and particularly they mention you. Now, did you ever receive any complaints from those refugees there, that they were being put into camps or put into centres and they were complaining that they were being ghettoised. They were being put in a ghetto. Were there complaints that were coming to you?

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I received letters from BH citizens who were in exile in third countries. I didn't analyse the letters, but I was greatly concerned and did my best to send them to the Ministry of Foreign Affairs in Sarajevo so that they could take further steps, if necessary. I cannot really remember that I received a letter of complaint from Denmark.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Were you aware that in Denmark, as in other places, as Mr. Rebic says, that accommodations of refugees were in separate centres? And in here, they're complaining that they're mostly isolated from the residential areas of the Danes. It is also a form of ghettoisation of our refugees, preventing them from getting closer to and acquainted with Danish life. Now, do those sorts of complaints come to you? And in your opinion, may I ask also, was the Danish way of treating the refugees, was that improper in any way, the fact that they were put into centres so that they could be watched upon and protected?

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really didn't give thought to things like that, either then or now, and I don't think my personal opinion is important here. I don't really know what you're interested in hearing. I never complained in my communication about how people were accommodated and things like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. I just want to make sure I'm clear then. So you have absolutely no complaints, before this Trial Chamber at least, as far as how the Muslim refugees were accommodated by the Republic of Croatia?

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I said, I sent out a separate report about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Ma'am --

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- with regard to the Gasinci and Obonjan conditions, and that they were all right in keeping with the regular standards.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. And what you're saying is that those camps -- those centres were sub-standard in your opinion?

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I claim, and I sent out reports, that the conditions of accommodation in both the camps that I reported on most frequently were in conformity with standards applied to refugees.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. All right. Now, I want to as though you another document, and this is 1D 01431. 1D 01431. This is dated -- if it's 1D, it's a Defence. If it's P, then it would be the big binder. Okay.

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I suspect you haven't seen this document, but you were aware that refugees were held in a place called Pinete; correct?

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I'm aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And I take it they were Croat refugees?

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the moment, when I went to visit Pinete, I was in contact with the Croats who had fled from the BH.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Now, here in this document, I only point this out in fairness, on 13th of April, 1994, if we go to the second paragraph, it says: "During the day, yesterday, Darinko Tadic had a meeting with the camp coordinators and leaders to discuss the beginning of the transfer of refugees from Pinete. The outcome of the meeting was that the camp coordinators resigned and said they were unable to persuade the refugees to move, and that they would not be responsible for the refugees if they decided to move." And then if you were to go on, it shows that two of the refugees went on a hunger strike? My question is: Were you aware that the Croatian government was also trying to -- to resettle or -- or move or transfer Croatian refugees, Croatian -- that is from Bosnia-Herzegovina, just as they had done with the Muslims who they tried to transfer from, say, apartments or hotels to centres? Were you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't know about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. You weren't -- okay. And this is the last -- the second to last paragraph, it says: "We warn you that they still refuse to be resettled; and according to reports from the MUP, several women have threatened to commit suicide if the move does not take place." It then goes on to say: "In the next few hours, we expect the refugees to step up their passive resistance, and it will probably be impossible to carry out the move peacefully. It will thus be necessary to -- to cooperate with the MUP and the Ministry of Defence. And in the case the operation continues, we request that you establish necessary coordination with superior officers in the MUP (Mr. Moric) and the Ministry of Defence (Mr. Vukina) in Zagreb. We urgently request instructions for further action." Now, this happened in 13 April 1994. We're talking about Croats from Bosnia-Herzegovina, which obviously the embassy would have been responsible for, and as you indicated were caring for or tried to care for. Is it your evidence that you were totally unaware of this action?

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Specifically, yes. As for Mr. Esterajher, concerning the same problems that were taking place but at a different locality, I certainly knew about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. But it seems to me though that the Croats from Bosnia-Herzegovina are treated pretty much the same as the Muslims from Bosnia-Herzegovina, the refugees, that is, at least from this letter. It seems, at least in Pinete, the Croats from Bosnia-Herzegovina are having to transfer out, just like the Muslims from Bosnia-Herzegovina had to do on occasion; correct?

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is what it written in this document, that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. All right. I'll move on. 1D 01582. And I just want -- this is a letter dated April 26, 1994. It's from Mr. Rebic. It's to a Mr. Fischer, and it says here: "Surviving winter office, Fischer." Did you know a Mr. Fischer by any chance?

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I met Mr. Fischer.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And, in fact, this particular document comes from you.

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: The document from Professor Adalbert Rebic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Right. But this was a document that we got from the Prosecution, that apparently either you or Ms. Turkovic turned over, but I just wanted to highlight a couple of points. On the first paragraph, it says: "Taking into account the permanent cooperation between your humanitarian organisation and the Office of Displaced Persons and Refugees of the Government of the Republic of Croatia, we would kindly request that you accept the changes in the procedure for issuing permits for transit through the Republic of Croatia." Now, we go on and it says here: "Namely, due to the frequent complaints from the Bosnia and Herzegovinian authorities claiming that this office, together with international humanitarian organisations, is helping the Serbians in the 'ethnic cleansing' of Bosnia and Herzegovina. In accordance with the embassy of Bosnia and Herzegovina in Zagreb, international humanitarian organisations must submit, with the request for acquiring permits for transit through the Republic of Croatia, a written concept from the Embassy of Bosnia and Herzegovina in Zagreb." Now, were you aware of this letter, and were you aware of these actions; that is, here is Mr. Rebic asking that consent first be granted or received by your particular embassy before there's any transfer. Were you aware of this?

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is the first time I see this letter, and it is it the first time that I hear that Dr. Adalbert Rebic believed that the embassy asked they should issue transit permits. This looks very strange to me, to tell you the truth.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Well, Mr. Rebic is not asking for your embassy to issue permits. They're asking for written consent. So -- because you and the others were complaining that the internationals and that Croats were assisting in the ethnic cleansing. So here he's asking Mr. Fischer, somebody you knew and worked with, to get written requests. That way there would be, a common word that we use here in court, "transparency." There would be no hidden agendas. Everybody would know exactly what was happening. Were you aware of these efforts by Mr. Rebic?

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is correct that we complained a great deal about what was happening with citizens from Bosnia-Herzegovina, but this is the first I hear that we asked for us to give consent, but I never knew of Mr. Rebic asking for something like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Very well. If we go to the next document, we're going to switch topics. This deals primarily with prisoners and the two centres we were talking about, 1D 01577. 1D 01577. It's dated September 20, 1993. It's addressed to a Mr. Hurtic.

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Did you know a Mr. Hurtic?

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I knew him. I know him, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And who was he?

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was also a staff member of the Embassy of Bosnia-Herzegovina in Zagreb.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Now, if you look at the first -- the second paragraph, it says here, basically, that there had been a meeting on the 20th of September, and that Dr. Granic on behalf of Franjo Tudjman, who was, you know -- that there was an implementation or that they agreed for the implementation of the joint declaration of the September 14, 1993, talks that had been held, and that there was a working group that was established and that there were certain agreements that were made. Were you aware of this working group? And this is in regards to refugee centre in Dretelj.

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Now, in the first -- in the paragraph under number 1, where it says, "We -- it was agreed as follows," it says: "The centre in Dretelj will be closed." And then if we skip -- I don't want to go -- spend too much time reading, but it says, "... 500 refugees accepted the offer of the Office of Displaced Persons and Refugees of the Republic of Croatia to be relocated in Obuljen and Gasinci." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Were you aware that this transfer was based on an agreement that was reached with this working group?

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is the first time I hear of it, or rather, that I see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And then it says, "The remaining 510 refugees will, in cooperation with the ICRC, be sent to adequate centres in Croatian Republic Herceg-Bosna." Were you aware of this?

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. We're going to set this document aside and we'll pick it up again shortly with the next topic, but we can now move on to the next document, and that would be 1D 01575. 1575. And this is dated August 13, 1993, and we see that it is -- it is signed at the end by a clerk in the Department of Refugees, Nametak Zejna.

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I am sure you know this -- this is a woman, right?

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's a lady. Yes, I know her.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: In fact, she worked closely with you, did she not?

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: She was in the department for refugees of the BH embassy.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Now, this document is relevant because of certain paragraphs that are in your statement -- in general would be paragraph 40, Your Honours, and then it would be 57, 58, and 59. But I just want to point out a couple of things in this letter -- or this information. One, it shows that the UNHCR had -- it says it has an office in Gasinci centre. Now, were you aware that UNHCR had an office in as opposed to around?

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was aware that the UNHCR was constantly present in Gasinci.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: That wasn't my question though. My question was whether you were aware that they had an office in. Being present means walking about maybe, going off and on, but having an office in means that they are there. Now, were you aware that they had an office there? It's sort of a yes or no or I can't remember answer.

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I received information. I was not in that office personally.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. So does that answer -- so is the answer to my question yes, they had an office in -- in the centre?

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Let me get this straight. Did you ever visit the centre?

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, many times.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. And you were able to walk around?

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. All right. And I take it that this individual, Ms. Zenja, she's a pretty responsible individual?

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was my assessment that she was responsible individual.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Now, if we go further down again, Your Honours, in the next paragraph we see again it says: "The UNHCR office in Gasinci ..." and I point that out, because I think it is relevant as to whether they have an office in as opposed to having an office by. Now, we've covered that, but let me go down, further down the page, because this is her assessment, and towards the second to last paragraph it says: "A special problem is caused by the immediate vicinity of the barracks of the Croatian Guard, and the refugees complain because of uncontrolled entry of guard members and militia and other persons of doubtful -- of doubtful moral values." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I see that paragraph.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Now, it doesn't say here, and I point this out and Their Honours can take it for whatever it's worth, it says nothing here about beatings or physical mistreatment as you have stated in paragraphs 57 and 58 of -- of your statement but, rather, it says that there was problem of uncontrolled entry of guards and other persons of doubtful moral values. And I take it that the doubtful moral values had to do with people that were probably engaged in drug trafficking. Would that be correct?

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what Mrs. Nametak meant by this. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And Your Honours on paragraph 59 of the statement the witness has indicated UNHCR had a branch office near, near, Gasinci in Djakovo. So I point that out, because here we have somebody from the embassy saying something different.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. We'll of move on. I don't think there's anything more -- well, there -- just this one -- if we go to the next -- the very last paragraph, I just want to point this out for the Trial Chamber. It says here that with the announcement of a possible return to the liberated areas in Bosnia and Herzegovina, the refugees have expressed a great interest in returning, so there has been a list compiled be consisting of 120 persons ready to return to Tuzla, Zenica, Mostar and Bugojno." And it says that: "The organisation for the return is being handled by the High Saudi Committee." Were you aware that there were people in this particular centre that wanted to return to Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. And -- all right. And I should also point out, I'm told, at the end of the second paragraph, Your Honours, where it says: "The majority of the citizens in transit are for Bosanska Krajina, Banja Luka, Prijedor, Kotor Varos," because earlier it says: "There are 900 citizens who do not have refugee status but are staying at the centre only as a transit point, but it would appear that the 900 are going to the Bosanska Krajina," and when we're talking about Banja Luka, Prijedor, and Kotor Varos, we're talking about the Republika Srpska. Right?

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: We're talking about the areas that the refugees came from originally, and they were under --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- the control of the Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. All right. If we go on to the next document very quickly, 7 -- this is 1D 01585. This is dated 7 October 1993. Okay.

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And it says here that this is from the International Committee of the Red Cross. And I take it you had contact with them?

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am sorry. The document is in the English language. I don't have it in the local language. I don't have a translation.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay --

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am sorry. It's here -- or, no, it's not. No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay no problem.

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: It seems to me there is only the English version.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. All right. Well, were you aware that the ICRC was prepared to participate in the implementation of the release of all detainees held by Croatian Defence Council simultaneously with the detainees of the Bosnian government, that they were willing to assist?

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: As for this particular information, I did have it but from the media.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Then we'll go on to the next. If we go on to the next document, 1D 01579. And if you find it. This is dated January 4, 1994. Do you have it, ma'am?

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do. I do have it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. If you go to the back, you'll see that it's signed by director of the RC Obonjan, and it's Miroslav Maslac.

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I see that it's his signature, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. You recognise the gentleman? You know the gentleman?

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know him.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And this letter is addressed to you, "dear Ms. Azra." Now I'm just going to read the first paragraph and then there is some other language in here that might be interesting, but it he says here: "For many days and nights I have been watching the tragedy of the Croatian and Muslim nations in the territory of the internationally recognised state of Bosnia and Herzegovina mute and desperate because of my own helplessness. I am aware that I cannot stop the tragedy, that my word is merely a silent whisper in the complete darkness, and I decided to contact you in order to ask you to use your position and the authority that you possess without any doubt, and contact Ms. Biserka Turkovic and other officials of the Presidency of BiH with solely one purpose: To stop the offensive and announce -- and announced [sic] bloodshed in the areas of Central Bosnia." And then if we go on further down, it -- again, he's asking you -- he's appealing to you to appeal to those in Bosnia-Herzegovina who are waging war in Central Bosnia to stop the madness that was going on. My question is: Did you receive this letter?

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really do not remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And I say -- so I take it if I were to ask you whether at any point in time you had contacted the authorities with respect to what he was asking you to do, and that is to stop the -- the activities that were happening in Central Bosnia where it would appear, at least, that the Croats were on the receiving end of the ethnic cleansing process --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PRANDLER
utterances.text: Mr. Karnavas.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PRANDLER
utterances.text: It is not critical. I would only like to make a correction in the record, and it is that when you said "to stop the offensive and announce -- and announced the bloodshed." I'm sure that it is "renounced," with an R.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I was reading literally, but you're probably right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Renounced, yes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Unfortunately, I tend to read what's on the paper.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: In any event, you don't recall whether you had contact with anybody based on letter, since you don't recall even receiving the letter?

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: My general firm position was that I was against any kind of bloodshed. As for the specific letter, I do not recall having received it, and, therefore, I do not know that I could have reacted -- or rather, I do not remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Very well. If we go on to the next document, 1D 01950. 1D 01950. In this particular document, we see that it's dated September 25, 1993, and the next set of documents deal with convoys and the working group. You were part of a working group, were you not, madam?

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, if we look at this document, what becomes rather obvious is that you, in this working group, are there on behalf or as a representative of the Muslim nation and not as a representative of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina. Would that be correct?

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: You are not right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: All the time, I felt to be the representative of the government of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Well, I point that out, because if you go into the middle of this document, it says: "The representatives of Croatian and Muslim nations." And when we look at who are the representatives, we see Zubak and Tadic, who are from the Bosnia and Herzegovina Croats, and then we see Azra Krajsek, Agovic, Jasarevic, and they seem to be for the Muslim nation. So at least with respect to this particular document, you're there in the working group as part of or on behalf of the Muslim nation; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is not correct. If you look at all my knowledge, I was, in full consciousness, the representative of the government of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and as such was a member of this group.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Could you point to me anywhere, then -- or let's look at the very last page. Maybe this will help us. The very last page, it's your signature there, is it not?

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, would it surprise you if I were to say, because we don't have the time, that in reading this document, nowhere in this document it says that you're there on behalf of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, or on behalf of the Embassy of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina; but, rather, the only references to you being there is as a representative of the Muslim nation, just as Mr. Zubak is there on behalf of the Croatian nation?

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I know is that I was appointed to the working group on the basis of an agreement between Presidents Izetbegovic and Tudjman, and that the Presidents of the States of Bosnia and Herzegovina and Croatia appointed the members of the working group.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Very well. If we look at -- we don't have much time to spend on this, but if we go to paragraph 7.3. I just want to point thought because I want to go back to an earlier document that we looked at. On 7.3 it says: "It is necessary to provide for written consent of the army of Bosnia and Herzegovina and HVO for undisturbed transit of the convoy through the territories under their control. With that purpose, it is suggested that all war activities cease while convoy is in transit." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't see it, but --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- as far as I followed the situation, that is something that I do know about. I haven't managed to find the actual paragraph, though.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: It is under the paragraph number 7, numbered 7.3. So that would be under --

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you. I can see it now.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, the reason I point that out is because if you go back to document 1D 01577, Your Honours, and madam, this was a document that we visited earlier. This was a letter from Mr. Pogarcic to a Mr. Hurtic from your embassy. We look at paragraph number 2, that's numbered 2, and we see here it says: "As regards the humanitarian convoy stationed in Stobrec, Split, as we are informed by the competent authorities of the Republic of Croatia and Croatian Republic Herceg-Bosna, for us there are no obstacles for departure. The Embassy of the RBiH in Zagreb should define the time of departure of the convoy by request to the Ministry of Interior of the Republic of Croatia, which has been done -- which has not been done so far. "I must inform you that the Muslim army started with fierce attacks on the whole front line from Mostar towards Central Bosnia, especially Vitez, on September 20, 1993," and it goes on and so on. Now, were you aware that, at least with respect to this issue, that they were waiting, from your particular embassy, documentation or some sort of an announcement as to the time of departure of the convoy?

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Because if we look at the very last sentence in this particular paragraph, it says: "Therefore, I suggest that the convoy for Gradacac," whatever, "from Stobrec is rerouted towards Zupanja for obvious reasons." So in other words, if we look at what precedes this, is that the ABiH is waging war. UNPROFOR has been notified. A convoy is ready to come. And in spite of what is happening, in other words, in spite of the ABiH, which was the Muslim army, for all, you know, as we know it, even though they were on the offensive, here you have Mr. Pogarcic suggesting an alternative route in order to get this convoy going, but it needed authorisation from your embassy. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can see what he's written, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Well, I know what he's written, but -- but this person, Mr. Hurtic, he would have been the responsible person to write to about these sorts of matters; right?

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Hold it, hold it, hold it, hold it.

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what he was responsible for.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: If you look at the top of it, it says "Mr. Zlatko Hurtic, attache coordinator for humanitarian activities." He's not addressing this to the janitor of the Embassy the Republic of Croatia -- of Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina. He's addressing this to the responsible person that's engaged with these sorts of issues; right?

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but you asked me why he was in charge of reporting, and my answer to that was that I didn't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Well, maybe -- maybe what I said was lost in translation, and this is not to say that it was mistranslated. But in any event, 1D 01591. This is a letter dated 25 November 1993, and it's addressed to a Mr. Raguz. You know Mr. Martin Raguz, or you knew of him? Right?

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I do apologise, but what's the document that we're looking at?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: 1D 01591. It's my fault. I'm asking you to look for a document while I'm also asking you questions.

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do have the document, yes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, here it is from the High Commissioner for Refugees, and here if we just look at the very first sentence, it says: "I would like to express my utmost satisfaction with the activities of the joint commission. Our convoy movements have been eased and in no way hindered since the commission was formed and the precise procedure of notifying was established." So it seems that, at least from this particular letter, things are working rather well, and Mr. Raguz is being complimented for his assistance. Were you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I apologise, but what is your question? Do you mean that I didn't know about the commission or the contents, the activities contained in this letter? If you're asking me that, then no, I was not aware of that. I didn't know about it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Karnavas, you've used up two hours, so who has been giving you additional time?

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I apologise for interrupting, but I'd like to request that you reconsider your decision about time given to the Defence teams for cross-examination. In view of the fact that this witness will be heard tomorrow as well, I think that it is far fairer to have the entire time intended for this witness spent in the courtroom, rather than keep to the decision about six hours of cross-examination which ruling was taken before the cross-examination began - allow me just to finish - and, in fact, that we have a statement with 121 articles. If we just ask two questions on each of these paragraphs, that would mean five minutes per paragraph which is 605 minutes altogether or ten hours. In addition to that, the Prosecutor tendered 37 documents. If we were to analyse each of these documents even superficially, this would take us another five hours extra. So we do need more time. I am going to give my time to Mr. Karnavas and to others who are dealing with this it, if I can put it civilian topic, but I with like to ask the Trial Chamber to enable Mr. Karnavas, at the expense of the joined time at our disposal, to complete his cross-examination; and if he is not able to do that, then I really will allot him all my time as well. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Fine. You're talking about 121 paragraphs in the written statement, but I'd like to remind you that the Chamber has stressed that amongst these paragraphs, you have paragraphs that are more or less relevant with respect to the indictment, so you don't need to review the entire statement. That's one point. The second point is that you're right, indeed, we still have one day tomorrow, but you should not forget that the Judges will ask questions, and we also have to take into account the redirect examination, and we have to be very careful in terms of the time we use. I would also like to have many hours to put questions to this witness, but I also take into account the fact that the accused are in detention at the moment and they are entitled to it an expeditious trial. Therefore, we need to focus on what's the most important, and that is what you are trying to do. Yes, Mr. Praljak.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, having dealt for many years with the problem of assistance by the Croatian state to the BH army and the Muslim people, on Thursday I brought to The Hague 95 binders - and I'm showing you a picture of all the binders because I can't bring them into court - with 10.000 documents in them dealing with all manner of topics: Education, refugees, the wounded, displaced persons, aid and assistance in support, the culture, the arming of the BH army, the training of the BH army, the units, their establishment, and so on and so forth. Unfortunately, here the indictment begins from the criminal enterprise of Franjo Tudjman. Now, these 95 binders, which we will bring into court willy-nilly at one point, can we at least go through some of the topics here? She won't know much about the army, but let's go through the education system. She might know some people, because there were over 30 persons who had the status of diplomatic representative who within her embassy dealt with the arming of the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina from the territory of the Republic of Croatia. I took part in it. I took part in it as assistant minister for providing Gasinci. The 3rd Brigade was in the less well-adapted part. So we help the army. I know every place where the weapons were stored, packed in tins sent in the UNHCR. We have the numbers who transported the weapons with the knowledge of Minister Susak and myself and the Croatian government. And we're faced here with a fact where you have to prove something, but I am ready. I have 95 binders, and many of these documents I wanted to deal with Ms. Azra. She visited Obonjan once. It's a pity that we only have one hour, and I must say it's almost impossible. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Just to briefly respond, Mr. President. First and foremost with the statement, if the Trial Chamber thinks that certain paragraphs are not relevant, then I think there's an obligation by the Trial Chamber, since they're going to curtail our time, there's an obligation, I stress that, to inform the parties which paragraphs it finds not relevant. That way the Prosecution can make whatever submissions it wishes to make on behalf of why certain paragraphs are relevant and perhaps should be considered; and on the other hand, the Defence would know what paragraphs the Trial Chamber feels to be not relevant. That way we don't have to waste our time. I indicated last time that a judicial hint would be welcoming in that fashion. Secondly, I wish to remind the Trial Chamber, as I did yesterday in a motion that I filed, it was a refiled motion on a motion for severance, that Mr. Prlic on occasions has waived his right to an expeditious trial, as it is understood by this Trial Chamber and other Trial Chambers; that is, a rather quick trial. And I noted in my one motion how in the Krajisnik case, Judge Orie indicated to Mr. Krajisnik that he was not going to hold it against him; in other words, this particular right. So Mr. Prlic is in no hurry of having a fast trial, but he wishes to have a very fair trial; and if it takes longer, so be it. I think we can all live with that. Be that as it may, I just wish to go on at this point. I'll try to go as fast as I can, keeping in mind that my colleagues also need time for themselves, having made my record.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Now, if I could go on to the next document just very -- well, we were interrupted, and you asked why I was asking you those questions. And the reason I'm going through this is because there seemed to be some insinuation on your part that humanitarian aid was not going back to Bosnia-Herzegovina. As I understand it, you said something about seven months there hadn't been a single convoy that had gone to Bosnia and Herzegovina. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is the information I had and that's what I said.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And here and that's why I pointed out this letter, it appears that you weren't aware of that. But let me show you 1D 01329. 1329. And -- and of course if we look at the bottom -- first of all, this is dated 10 December 19 -- well, it indicates the passage approved for the following convoys from 1 June 1993 till 10 December 1993. 1 June to 10 December. And this is from the office of refugees and expelled persons of HR HB. If we look at the bottom we see some initials, MR, and there's a signature. On the second page we see a signature line, and it's Martin Raguz. And we see on the very first page total convoys 1.399, and then on the second one we see Jablanica, and we have 2.000 -- I mean -- it's 25.847. This is -- we're talking about tonnes. What's more telling, however, is the list that we see. And we don't have time to go through the list, but would it surprise you to learn - and the Trial Chamber can verify this, they can do an accounting - that at least from June -- June 15th until September 23, 1993, based on these statistics, and perhaps Mr. Raguz will come either from the Prosecution or from the Defence to verify this, that we have 193 convoys going through. Would that surprise you, madam? Were you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I was not aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Do you think -- well, let me ask you something else, because in reading your statement early this morning, I re-read it again, and something caught my eye again, and that is you made a statement here saying that -- in your statement you indicate that you had no dealings or no contacts with the officials of HZ HB, the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna, or -- and then later on with the Croatian Republic of Herceg-Bosna. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, may I ask, is there a reason why in light of the fact, in light of the fact, and here's the tripwire, that President Izetbegovic, the president of the Presidency, along with others who are representing the Muslim nation, were having talks and discussions with members and officials of the Croatian nation of officials of the Croatian republic or the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna, and in fact a lot of those discussions were not -- were held also with the internationals and in Zagreb. So is there a particular reason why you in the embassy of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, supposedly representing all of the people of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, why you did not have any contact with any officials?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Your Honour, I just want to register an objection to the form of the question. It's Mr. Karnavas's characterisation that Mr. Izetbegovic was the president of the Muslim nation. That's his characterisation. The Prosecution does not agree with that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I indicated that he was the president of the Presidency --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Of the Muslim--

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: -- of the SDA.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I'm reading --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: He was representing the Muslim nation that's the difference. He was the president of the Presidency, but we also had testimony and I remind Your Honours of Mr. Okun, Ambassador Okun. It was very clear Silajdzic, Ganic, all of them were representing the interests of the Muslim nation and the army of ABiH was the military arm of the SDA. I think that's uncontroverted.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I don't think that's the case, but I waive my objection, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I leave it to the Court.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Exactly. I'll leave it to the entire trial record on there. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Question: Is there any reason why you didn't have any contact with them? Were you forbidden, were you instructed not to, or was this something out of a personal choice?

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was not instructed. I didn't deal with matters of choice, but nobody tried to contact me or call me up at all and that was the reason that I had no contact.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Very well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, Mr. Karnavas asked you the question I wanted to put to you yesterday. You were working at the embassy. You were a member of the embassy. Amongst the Judges here you have two former ambassadors. We know perfectly well that when you work in an embassy your first task is to have contacts with the officials of the country where you are serving, and you don't sit there waiting for people to get in touch of you. It's up to the embassy to get in touch with the outside, to make contacts. You, apparently, were in charge of all humanitarian questions. Why didn't you take the initiative of taking contacts or making contacts with the Croatian officials who could have helped you in your task?

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was in permanent contact with them, the Office for Displaced Persons and Refugees, especially, and also with the Ministry of Foreign Affairs. I had contacts with them and the staff of the Ministry of Foreign Affairs of the Republic of Croatia, and all the other officials, but I understood it that I was asked why I didn't have contacts with institutions of the HZ HB. And believe me when I say, I didn't even know that they existed, that they were official bodies and had representative offices in the Republic of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You had never heard of this body called the Republic of Herceg-Bosna? You'd never heard of that body?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I knew that an HZ HB entity existed, but I didn't know that this HZ HB entity had its office in the Republic of Croatia, or offices. So I understood that you were asking me why I didn't contact -- have contacts with that particular office.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Karnavas.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. You had contacts with the Sarajevo government?

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Mostar was in Bosnia and Herzegovina at the time? Still is, by the way.

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And so you knew where to contact any of the officials of the HZ HB or the HR HB if you wanted to; correct?

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, I was the attache for refugees.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Exactly. With respect to refugee issues, if you needed to or if you wanted to contact, because after all refugees were coming from Herzegovina, okay, whether it was Central Bosnia or Herzegovina, okay, from areas that were within the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna, okay, if you wanted to get in contact with them, you knew how to; correct?

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, and I did come into contact with institutions who were responsible for taking care of them, and they were institutions of the host country.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Okay. Well, I just want to -- no, it's not whatever. The point is I'm asking you about the Croatian Community. I'm not asking you about Croatia. Because it seems to me, ma'am, that when you see a Croat, wherever he comes from, you think that he should be represented by the Croatian Republic, right, from the Republic of Croatia. Is that your opinion?

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm very surprised that you can think that you know what I am thinking.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Well -- well, I'm asking you because -- I'm asking you because you were dealing with Mr. Zubak. You were dealing as the representative of the of Muslim nation. Mr. Zubak was the representative of the Croatian nation. You had three nations, plus others, recognised in Bosnia-Hercegovina, and my question is: How is it that you, as a representative of the embassy, dealing with refugee matters in Croatia or dealing with citizens of Bosnia and Herzegovina, which included Croats from Bosnia and Herzegovina, how is it that you chose not to have any contact with, based on your statement, of authorities of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna, keeping in mind that Izetbegovic, Silajdzic, Ganic, and others were having contacts with those officials, be it Mate Boban, be it others, dealing with all sorts of issues including issues dealing with refugees? So how is it that you chose not to have any contact with officials from the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna? What is your explanation?

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was always very decisive and resolute on the fact that I would have contacts with all institutions that were open and that existed and were open to providing assistance, protection to the refugees of Bosnia and Herzegovina in Croatia. So I maintained contacts with all those institutions. I never made any decisions deciding that I would contact the HZ HB institutions, but they could not have had access to solving BH refugee problems in the host country, so I didn't need to contact them. It wasn't a matter of a decision on my part. There was no decision-making in that sphere.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Very well. I'll -- I think I'll accept that answer, for whatever it's worth. 1D 01589. If you could look at this document which may tie into what we've been discussing. 1D 01589. This is a document that's dated May 31, 1993. At the very top, you see that it's from the Embassy of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, Zagreb. If we look at the second page, we see a signature and we also see the official stamp, and this has been signed by Ms. Turkovic. Do you see this, madam?

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can see the document. I have it, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And if we look at the very top part, we see that it says: "Mr. Jadranko Prlic, mandator of the government of Bosnia-Herzegovina," and then there's a fax number, so at least you have no how to contact him, or Ms. Turkovic knew how to contact him. Were you aware of this letter, and were you aware of what capacity Mr. Jadranko Prlic was serving as mandator of the government of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've never seen this letter before. I do know that Mr. Jadranko Prlic was a politician with a lot of authority and credibility. Now, what post he held exactly, I never knew. I wasn't interested. I mean, I didn't deal with things like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: If we go to 1D 01588, 1d 01588, dated May 31, 1993, and this is from the office of the president of the government of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, and here it says: "We attach a letter from the embassy of the RBiH in Zagreb that is arrived addressed to me but also sent to high representatives of the International Peace Conference on the former Yugoslavia and UNPROFOR. The letter requests the provision of air transport for wounded persons from the left bank of the Neretva River and our assistance is requested." And then later on it -- you see in the second paragraph, it says: "I ask for your full cooperation ..." And this was sent to your embassy. Were you aware of these efforts by Dr. Jadranko Prlic to the letter that was sent by Ambassador Turkovic to Dr. Jadranko Prlic, as well as to Lord David Owen and others?

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, but I did know that these problems were dealt by other departments. So I didn't necessarily have to be informed of this, and I've never seen this document before. This is the first time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, were you aware that Dr. Jadranko Prlic was engaged in any capacity with the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna or the Croatian Republic of Herceg-Bosna? Were you aware of that at that time? I know you were in Zagreb, but were you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I knew that he was some high-ranking official; but to be quite frank, I don't know what post he held.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Very well. Now, if we could just very quickly, and I just want to -- somewhat relevant to this topic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We are at about time for the break. How many more minutes do you need?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: If I could go -- I think I need five minutes, Your Honour. Five minutes, and I think I could -- I'll just -- I can leave it -- if I have five minutes, I can finish up and then leave my time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Fine. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Just very quickly, just two documents back to back: 1D 01586, and then I'll be looking at 1587. So if we look at those documents very quickly. The date is May 21, 1993. So that would be ten days earlier. And this is in regards to a goodwill mission from the Republic of Turkey. Were you aware of this goodwill mission at or about that time?

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Were you keeping track of any activities that were happening no Bosnia-Herzegovina, or were you just so focused in Croatia that you didn't know what was happening in Central Bosnia or Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I can tell you that at that time, I was working 15 hours a day --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: So the answer is no?

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- at a minimum, in order to deal with problems related to Croatia and the refugees in Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I'll take that as a --

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I couldn't answer yes or no, because neither would be accurate.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Very well. You weren't aware of this. But here in both of these letters, both of these documents, 1D 01586 and 1587, we see that Dr. Jadranko Prlic signs as President of the government of RBiH, and he's asking for cooperation and assistance. And I take it, from your answer, you simply don't know anything about any of this. If the answer is no, I'll just move on.

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Now, going back to it a question that was asked by Judge Trechsel yesterday, and I did see one document that sort of caught my interest, and that was 10049. It's a Prosecution document. 1 -- 1 -- it's a big binder.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Mr. Usher, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: 10049. And this is in regards to a question with respect to people going back and forth, vacationing in a sense, visiting family members, that sort of thing. 10049. It's dated 21 April 1993. It's a letter to the RBH embassy in RH, which would be the Republic of Croatia, from the RBH military mission in the Republic of Croatia, Split desk. So this is a military -- this is generated by the military. And I just wanted us to look at a couple of things. First is, in the first paragraph, we see that it says: "There are approximately 130.000 citizens of Bosnia and Herzegovina registered in the general area of Dalmatia. We estimate that among them are a large number of men liable for military service staying here for various reasons (official visits, approved visits to families, drivers and staff working for humanitarian organisations, wounded persons and persons staying without permission of relevant RBH organs)." My question is who are -- who would grant the permissions? Who are these organs, the RBH organs, that would grant these relevant permissions or these permissions that would -- you know. Do you know them? Which organs --

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really don't know. I know when I went out on official trips what the authorities -- what authorities I had to contact in order to get permission to travel on business.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Was the military mission in Split complaining that there were some men of military age or conscripts who were more or less deserting, for lack of a better term, or vacationing or not doing what they were supposed to be doing back in Bosnia-Herzegovina? Was that a complaint?

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not as far as I'm concerned. I mean, not to the office for refugees that I had.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. So you had no knowledge of that. Okay.

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I had no knowledge about what it was that they were --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- reporting about.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And one last aspect of this document. If you go to page 2 and if we go to the first paragraph, because I'm told that this may be somewhat relevant, and I'll start reading: "Because of the blockade, a lot of people and equipment are prevented from returning safely to Bosnia and Herzegovina in their original units, -- in their original units," I point that out for the Judges, "while nearly all their HVO permits valid for Republic of Croatia have expired. For this reason over 1.000 men," and here in English it says, "fit for military service," but I'm told it should read, "conscripts," "and many more refugees have contacted our desk VI in Split indirectly or in person. We have noticed that all men fit for military service are filled with panic, fear and uncertainty as a result of numerous provocations and incidents and -- incidents that they and their families have been exposed to, including physical abuse, arrests, and taking away of our citizens." Now, were you aware that there were -- that there were over 1.000 conscripts, Muslim conscripts, in Croatia at that time while there was a war waging next door?

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. One final question and we could take our break and I'll be through. Yesterday you indicated -- a question was posed to you by the Prosecutor regarding the Mujahedin. Were you aware that there were Mujahedin in Central Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I heard from refugees that they had heard that Mujahedin would come.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: That's not my question. My question: Did you know that they were there? And I say this because we have footage of -- of the president of the Presidency, Mr. Alija Izetbegovic, we see him there while they're chanting. There are photographs. The world knows about it. And in fact, in a courtroom next door soon Mr. Delic, General Delic, is going to be prosecuted, and the Mujahedin are a central theme into that Prosecution. So I'm asking you. Were you aware, were you personally aware that there were Mujahedin in Central Bosnia? Answer yes or no.

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. And so when the refugees told you that the Mujahedin were there or that they had been told that they were there and coming, did you believe them, or did you think this was something that was made up in order to scare them to leave?

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Before I thought that they were scaring them with that, saying that the Mujahedin would appear. I did not really believe in that myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Did you ever come to learn, however, the atrocities they were committing and how they committed them in order to scare them? Did that ever come to -- did you ever learn of that later on?

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Much later, when the war was over. When communication and information went up. When information was publicly provided. And that provided for the possibility that this was not an erroneous announcement. However, at the time when I received this information, I had no knowledge of my own, and to tell you the truth, I did not believe in this.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Thank you, ma'am.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Fine. We'll take a 20-minute break, and we'll resume at 11.00.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, as a matter of courtesy, I think it is only right for me to say that we have a new trainee here in the courtroom, Stjepan Rako. He's a residence of the Republic of Netherlands, and he is Croatian by origin. Thank you.
