utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I wish your new trainee welcome here. Ms. Nozica, you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. Good morning to all in the courtroom. Before I start, I would like to inform the Court that I have one hour of time. That is the time that was allocated to me for cross-examination, and have an hour that I got from the Coric Defence. I would now like to ask for the usher's assistance to give the binder of documents to the witness and to the Prosecutors.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Ms. Krajsek.

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: This is already your third day --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Nozica, I was looking at the report. You have one hour of your own time, but you only have 30 minutes from Mr. Coric, because Mr. Coric had granted you 30 minutes -- or rather, had granted 30 minutes to Mr. Karnavas. So you have one hour and 30 minutes in total.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Thank you. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Ms. Krajsek, several times, during the course of these three days, you said that you knew roughly about the statistics, about the number of refugees and displaced persons who, from the beginning of the war, in Bosnia-Herzegovina in this Croatia. You probably saw some of them during the course of your work, and, obviously, you knew some things because the relevant statistics were published. Am I right?

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: I believe it would be important for us to deal with a specific document. That is the second document in your binder. That is 2D 4 -- 2D 00486. So that is the second document in your binder.

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have the document, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: As we can all see, this is a document of the government of the Republic of Croatia, the Office for Refugees. We see that the date is the 12th of June, 1998, and it says here who it was sent to; that is to say, government of the Republic of Croatia, the Office for Cooperation with the International Criminal Tribunal. So this is our source. This has to do with refugees and displaced persons from the period of 1992 to 1998 in the Republic of Croatia. Now, I'm going to go with some of the -- with you through some of the statistics where you may have some indirect knowledge, and also the period about which you certainly have direct knowledge. I would just like to say that the document was given to the interpreters as well, and I think that we will be able to go through these important matters quickly. The first part deals with information about the population of Bosnia and Herzegovina in 1991, and all of us in this courtroom are more or less familiar with this. And now I'd like to move on to the other part, and it has to do with the UNHCR information about refugees from Bosnia-Herzegovina. The first sentence says: "According to UNHCR information, there were 1.8 million displaced persons and refugees from Bosnia-Herzegovina in 1995 distributed as follows: 900.000 displaced persons within Bosnia-Herzegovina, 200.000 refugees in FRY refugees in third countries, western Europe and countries across the ocean. By the end of 1997, according to UNHCR information, some 400.000 refugees and displaced persons came back to Bosnia and Herzegovina which included almost 300.000 people from third countries." Are you aware of this information? This is UNHCR information. I know that up until the end of August 1994 you were at that post in charge of refugees in Croatia, but I imagine that you expressed some interest later on as well for these figures.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreters note they have great trouble hearing the speaker could she please speak into the microphone. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We tend to say that regardless of what I did afterwards, I always kept an eye on this matter. I more or less always knew what was going on in terms of these statistics.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: It interpreters note, it is the counsellor who is a problem for us, not the witness. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Now I would ask you to move on to paragraph 3. So it's on the next page. It has to do with refugees from Bosnia-Herzegovina in the Republic of Croatia. Are things all right with my microphone now? Can you hear me better?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreters note yes thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: I hope things will be better now and we are moving on to refugees of Bosnia-Herzegovina in the Republic of Croatia and this is information by years. I think that you have already said that you are aware of this particular piece of information that towards the end of 1992 in Croatia there were about 300.000 refugees and the actual figure is 371.319 refugees from Bosnia-Herzegovina out of which in terms of their status we are talking about the end of 1992 285.630 of them had refugee status and 85.689 of them did not have that status. Until the end of 1992, large groups of refugees entered Croatia and it was not possible to register all of them by giving them --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Excuse me. I didn't want to rudely to interrupt you, but I cannot help noticing that if I add 285.000 and 85.000, I do not -- I get quite considerably above the 300.000 total. I get then to about 370.000. So something -- something must be wrong. Out of 300.000, it is not possible that 285.000 have the status and another 85.000 do not. I think you wish to clarify.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 371.319 refugees in December 1992. However, I would like to ask you, Your Honour, we are going to have tables here as well. Now, I'm talking about figures because they are relevant as well, but we will see them through the relevant statistics. So you will be able to compare all these figures, and you will see that they are all tally in terms of what is written in this report. So all the way up to the end of 1992, large groups of refugees were coming to Croatia. So it was not possible to register all of them in terms of registering them as persons having the status of refugees?

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: You agree with that, don't you? They were not coming in organised fashion at that time. People were fleeing, and it is certain that not everyone could be registered straight away.

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I agree with what you said.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: In addition to that, in the SFRY, in December 1992, there were 31.449 refugees from the FRY. You don't need to know all of this, but it does seem logical in view of the fact that the war broke out then.

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would not like to answer questions that are related to pure statistics, because then I can only talk about my feeling, and that is not an acceptable criterion.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Ms. Krajsek, I'm going to ask you to kindly give me an answer. This is a very important document. During the first day of our cross-examination, the Judges asked us whether we had this information. I'm just asking you to give me answers in terms of what you know, and you can freely say, I think that would be about it. I mean, even if we were to ask the author of this text about this now, I think he could not give accurate figures. In May 1993, when -- after the re-registration of refugees, 271.096 refugees from Bosnia-Herzegovina had refugee status in May 1993 in Bosnia-Herzegovina -- from Bosnia-Herzegovina; then it says part of them left for Western European countries and a smaller part did not keep their refugee status or they returned to Bosnia-Herzegovina. Now we are talking about the period when you were in Zagreb; right?

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: So, more or less, you could be aware of this piece of information?

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Then it says, in December 1993, there were 282.728 refugees in Croatia. I'm going to skip a paragraph now. And then it says, according to information of the 22nd of July, 1994, in Croatian, there were 30.000 refugees from Central Bosnia and other areas of the conflict between Croats and Muslims. They consisted of 30.000 Croats and 3.000 Muslims, approximately. That is the period while you were still in Zagreb. Can you say something about this, at least in approximate terms about these figures?

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: They seem logical to me.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: All right. Now we're going to move on to paragraph 2. It says, out of the total of 271.096 of refugees in Croatia, in May 1993, after the registration of refugees was carried out, there were 110.634 Croats, which is to say, 40.81 per cent; then 157.066 Muslims, which is 57.93 per cent; 1.272 Serbs, which is 0.47 per cent; and 2.124, that is say, 0.78 per cent members of other national minorities. We are talking about some statistics from May 1993. Did your embassy and your office within the embassy ever deal with such matters; that is say, the ethnic composition of refugees in terms of the statistics. And can you confirm this information, to the best of your knowledge, what we see here?

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I asked the Office for Expellees and Refugees to receive information about refugees registered in the Republic of Croatia. In this first stage, I did receive statistics from the office.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Does that information tally roughly with what I said?

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, it could be that or something similar.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Thank you. Further on, it says: "Before that, at the end of 1992, there were 60 to 70 per cent of Muslims among the refugees. The percentage of Croats and Muslims started to change at the end of 1993 and during the following years. At the end of 1993, new Croat refugees came to Croatia from Central Bosnia." I think that you testified about that too; right?

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Now, why did this decrease take place? And it's the next paragraph. The most important reason for the reduction of the number of refugees in Croatia in May 1993, when compared to the number of -- number at the end of 1992, is the large departure of refugees towards third countries. At first, in summer, autumn of 1992, the Western European countries and overseas countries had quotas for taking in refugees. You were not in Zagreb, but I think that you knew about that. I think we all knew that America, Australia had certain quotas set and certain priorities in terms of immigration into these countries. Are you familiar with that? ?

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: It was primarily Muslim refugees who left Croatia in accordance with entrance policies of western countries who introduced a rationed and selective acceptance of BH refugees. They accepted primarily ex-prisoners from Serbian camps, mixed marriages, et cetera. Can you and I add younger people to this category, that that was a category that they took in?

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Intellectuals were also welcomed as well.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Yes, yes. The last paragraph, through those programmes of transfer into foreign countries, western European and overseas countries from the 1st of October 1992 to the end of May 1998 42.076 refugees left Croatia, and they were mostly Muslims according to UNHCR information. And then the text explains why there was a small portion of Croats and it's precisely due to these criterias. It says Croats could not meet the criteria because Croats from Bosnia-Herzegovina had dual citizenship and the countries of immigration generally believe that Croatians from Bosnia-Herzegovina had yet another homeland that could take care of them. However, it is also fair to add that quite a few Croats left, especially families of guest workers who had already been living and working in Germany. Does that correspond to your own knowledge?

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: It is a generally known fact and you and I can conclude that perhaps Germany was one of the countries that took in the largest number of refugees from Bosnia-Herzegovina, not taking into account the ethnic background of these refugees at all. Is that your knowledge as well?

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think so, yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Very well. Then the text says at the end of 1992 between 65 and 70 per cent of refugees were Muslims. In 1993 that percentage changed to 58 per cent in 1993 around 40 per cent in 1994 and around 25 per cent in 1995 most of the refugees in 1995 were Croat refugees from Bosnia-Herzegovina and this is roughly what you said; that this number of Muslims if we proceed from those who originally came in 1992 the number actually went down. That corresponds to your own knowledge. Am I right or am I not right?

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: In part.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: When you say "in part," I wish you would say where it is that I'm right in part?

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: As in terms of the overall figures that I mentioned, but I use that number as the total number of Bosnian citizens who had fled not only Muslims. I really did not know of any other figures, so I couldn't have provided anything else.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: I know what information you provided and I know that you received some of this information that you agree with that as far as 1993 is concerned so I'm just asking. I'm not saying that you're the person who actually carried out this analysis, but I'm just asking you that on the basis of all this information that you got and on the basis of your personal knowledge did you know, for example?

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Total numbers in structure, no.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could speakers please slow down thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: It says further on in the text and this is very important until at the end of 1992 or until the end of 1992 large groups of refugees poured into Croatia week after week, and at the same time large groups left Croatia for European countries. So it was hard to follow the situation of all the refugees from Bosnia-Herzegovina and all the official information lagged after the actual situation. At that time, there was a constant ratio of 30 per cent of refugees who were not registered. Now, madam, does this seem to you to be logical?

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. But could you please tell me -- may I ask you something? Could you give me the number of the paragraph that you're reading from?

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: You moved on to page 2 of the text, and I'm reading that second paragraph on this page of yours.

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Last sentence. "The number of refugees began to stabilise only at the beginning of 1993 and it was then that the office undertook the first registration of refugees." Is that what you knew about?

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I knew that the registration took place at that time.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Now, we have information here for April 1995 and for statistical purposes that attends this analysis, I'm just going to read some of the facts, some figures, and tell me if you know about them because you'd already left at the time, it says: "In April 1995 Croatia had 185.428 refugees from Bosnia-Herzegovina and once again we have a national structure here or national breakdown where it says consisting of 134.086 Croats, 47.880 Muslims and the rest were Serbs and members of other ethnic groups. " And then we have another figure, that is to say, the number of refugees who came in from the territory of the federation and that is 75.456 and from the areas that were under the control of the Serbs in Bosnia-Herzegovina and that figure is 109.864.

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm very sorry, but please don't ask me about 1995 because I really can't address that.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Can we then conclude with looking at paragraph 4 which speaks of 1993, so we can go back to that period; although, it goes on until the 31st of May 1996. But it says: "From 1993 until the 31st of May, 1996, Croatia received 40.161 refugees, mostly from areas of Bosnia-Herzegovina under Serbian control on the basis of entrance permits that were issued by the Office for Refugees and Displaced Persons." Now, did you know about that? Were you aware of that? And in your contacts with the refugees, did you hear about information both refugees and Croats and Muslims who came from the area controlled at the time by the army of Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: I'd now like to ask you to look at something that I think you ought to know about, the last paragraph of that page where it says, "From the summer of 1995 until July 1996 there were some 20.000 Muslim refugees from Velika Kladusa and Cazin were accommodated in Kupljensko in the Republic of Croatia. Now, do you know anything about that? And we're dealing with some general facts. It is the time of the conflict between the 5th Corps of the BH army Fikret Abdic's forces.

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do know about that. Prior to my return to Bosnia-Herzegovina, on one occasion, I visited these people. They were displaced persons. Actually, they were in no man's land in between the two countries in the Kupljensko in Croatia. They hadn't gone into Croatia yet, and they hadn't left BH yet.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Now, if we look at the last sentence of that paragraph, where it stays that the camp was closed at the beginning of 1996, when in May 1996, when the refugees moved out and were relocated?

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really don't know if it was in the media then, probably, but I didn't listen to the news on a regular basis. I listened to it selectively.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: I asked you about that because you spoke of considerably -- you spoke a lot about these two places, and we see that these refugees were relocated there, too, the ones who came --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Ms. Nozica, could you please enlighten the Chamber on the relevance of these figures from 1966 for our work -- or 1996 for the work of the Chamber? It seems a bit far-fetched to me. You certainly have a good explanation but I'd like to know it.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I don't have any exceptionally good explanation, except to say the analysis before you comprises a period which is relevant to the indictment, but some facts and figures do not go up -- do not include only the period which is relevant to the indictment. So it says, as we can see, it ranges from 1993 to 1996. So as we're interested in a set period of time between those two dates, I really can't say. I wasn't the person who compiled these statistics. But we will, of course, be showing facts and figures which concentrate on the period we're interested in, and what I wanted to know was the efforts undertaken by Croatia - I'm sure Mr. Praljak will do that - as far as the refugees in Bosnia-Herzegovina are concerned throughout the time period in the indictment. And that is something that this witness can testify to because most of these refugees who arrived in 1992 are ones she came across when she came to take up her post in 1993, but I will skip over the portions which relate to 1996.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: So now, Witness, may we go on to point 10 of this analysis, and there we have something that is very important. And it is the table jibing the situation and everything we've been talking about. So, as I say, we have a chart there which shows us what the situation was like in December 1992, that's what it starts off with, and the total number. And we saw from the analysis that in 1992, the office did not have all the statistical data at its disposal. Now we can see May 1993. That's the next entry and the figure there is 271.096. That's the total, and here it just shows the figures for Croats and Muslims; then we go on to 1995, 1996, and 1997. We're not going to deal with those now. And that would more or less correspond to what we read out in the analysis; isn't that right, Witness?

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Now let's move on to the fourth part of this analysis, which is page 6 of the Croatian, and in the English we don't have the page numbers, but it comes after point 14. And the heading of that chapter is "Dynamics of the Refugee Crisis," the survey. It's section 4, and it speaks about the first arrivals of refugees from Bosnia-Herzegovina to Croatia in April 1992. That's the first paragraph. The second paragraph speaks of the refugee wave at the end of May and beginning of June, the expulsion of the population from various areas, and so on and so forth. And now I'd like to look at the penultimate paragraph, where it says, "The first columns of refugees from Bosnia-Herzegovina are moving towards Croatia." That means we're dealing with May 1992 and the waves are spiralling, the refugee waves are spiralling. And we see between 1 and 2.000 refugees pouring into Croatia every day. Large groups of refugees arrived in Croatia after the occupation of Bosanska Posavina and Jajce at the end of 1992. . And the last paragraph says, "In March 1992, the refugees from Bosnia-Herzegovina in Croatia numbered 16.000-odd, 16.579 to be exact. And at the end of that year, we have 371.319 refugees, and I'm sure you know that that was the situation, if not in absolute figures, but you realise that this figure of 371.000-odd was the result of the war in Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that corresponds to what I know.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Thank you. Now let's look at page 7. So it's that same section, that same chapter. I'd just like to ask you whether you know about this. It says, "After the appeal, the government of the Republic of Croatia in July 1992 to the European countries to take in Bosnian refugees, and a part of large column of refugees from Bosnia-Herzegovina through Croatia is moving towards the west across Croatia two-third countries, and about 450.000 refugees went that way. But before that, according to certain statistical data, they spent time in Croatia on an average of three months." Now, can you tell us whether this is something you knew about?

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: After the events, I did receive information to that effect.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Now let's move on to the next page, which is page 8 in the Croatian version. In English,, let me just say that it is chapter 5 entitled, "The Welfare System for the Refugees and Displaced Persons in Bosnia-Herzegovina." And the number in English is 2D 380118. It's already on e-court. Yesterday, during your testimony, you said - and I took note of that on page 39, lines 13 to 16 - that this organisation -- or rather, that the organisation of the Department for Refugees and Displaced Persons, according to the different regions, is something you knew about.

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did know that they had local offices.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: I'm reading the first sentence. It says, "At the end of 1992, in order to take care of the refugees, Croatia organised a special system by connecting the already existing system of welfare sentence with a newly formed Office for Refugees and Displaced Persons." And it says that 22 regional offices for refugees and displaced persons were organised, and that would correspond more or less to what you knew about; is that right?

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't tell you the exact number, but yes, I do know that a lot of offices were opened throughout Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Yes. They probably opened successively as the need arose?

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, if your point isn't to give an exact figure, then I can agree with you.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Yes, quite right. That's what I was after. Now let's look at paragraph 4, which speaks about money issues. So let's just make an introduction. It says, "The Office for Refugees and Displaced Persons of the government of Croatia takes care of refugees and displaced persons through the national fund or republican found called Kralj Zvonimir, which is financed from the national budget." Did you have any about that?

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did hear of the King Zvonimir Fund.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Right. Now we can move on to chapter six, on the next page, entitled, "Financial Expenditure for the Welfare of Refugees and Displaced Persons in the period between 1992 and 1997." And that is the English page 2D 38-01169. We have here facts and figures, and I think you said that statistics isn't a strong point of yours when it comes to money, how much money Croatia spent on refugees from the budget and so on.

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't know about that.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Nonetheless, let's go through this or parts of this section to see -- and we're talking about funds which Croatia received from the UNHCR, the European Community and various donations. Let's see if something rings a bell. It says, "Most of the expenses for the accommodation of refugees and displaced persons in the Republic of Croatia were made by the state, the Croatian state. From 1991 until the end of 1997, Croatia spent more than 1.603 billion US dollars on refugees and displaced persons, including the expenses of health care, schooling, et cetera. Of that sum, 1.133 billion US dollars were used for basic care for refugees and displaced persons, 718 million US dollars for displaced persons, and 415 million US dollars for refugees." I'd now like to move down two paragraphs, and it says, "From the budget of Croatia, the Republic of Croatia from 1992 to 1997, the national fund was the channel for the realisation of this, and the figure was 5.651.000 Kunas. Kunas aren't relevant. Let's go to dollars. And it is it is 897.020.658-odd US dollars. And then it says, "The total international financial help for the care of refugees and displaced persons donated through the office for refugees and displaced persons amounted to a total of 227 million US dollars. And then it goes on to break this down for welfare, settlements for refugees and displaced persons, and partly for renovation. And now we come to an important part: The contribution of international help for refugees and displaced persons never rose above 30 per cent in relation to the sums spent from the Croatian budget and its contribution in the period from 1992 to 1997 is 11 per cent on an average. Now, you might know this. It says: "Through the National Kralj Zvonimir Fund from 1992 to 1997 international humanitarian programmes of the UNHCR, the European Union, the Norwegian government" --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Nozica, sorry for interrupting, but we are perfectly capable of reading the document. What would be more interesting would be for you to put questions to the witness rather than reading out portions of the text and ask the witness to -- the witness to say yes. We are perfectly able to read the document. What we want from the witness is for her to tell her -- tell what she says -- what she knows about the events. So ask her whether she knew about funding and she can say, Yes or No. If she says No, then move on to something else. Well, of course, if you want to spend your time that way that's your choice.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I've just done that. Perhaps you didn't notice, but I did just ask the witness and say that we are moving on. The witness said she didn't know, and I will ask questions about this. But I was just asking the witness whether she knew about these facts and figures provided by the UNHCR, the European Union, and so on and so forth. And I'll tell you of the sums. Here it says that the UNHCR donated 82.661 -- or rather 82.661.978 US dollars. Do you know about that? Or do you know anything at all about how much the UNHCR donated to dealing and caring for refugees and displaced persons.

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Counsel, I have to apologise. This is maybe a professional deformation, because I'm an auditor and I memorise auditing data from confirmed official sources. Now, I don't want to say about -- anything about this, what I heard, what I read. I really didn't focus my attention on information of this kind so I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Well, can we look at the end of this document together linked to this information as you say. It is signed by the head and it says all the above facts and figures are official information of the Office for Refugees and Displaced Persons of the government of the Republic of Croatia and most of the official information appeared in official publications published by the Croatian government. So can you testify that you might have seen some of these facts and figures in official Croatian sources? About the number of refugees, the number of funds, the structure and so on and so forth?

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I said yes official information published by Croatian institutions, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you. Could you tell us did you see that?

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: For the transcript, we have to say that attached to this document is Document 2D 00494; namely, information that pertains to table 10 of this report pertaining to April 1995. Madam, I am not going to go through this with you. I just want the transcript to reflect this. Now we have document 487, statistical information about the ethnic structure of refugees. Paragraph 3 of this report speaks about that, the document is 2D 00488. That is information in paragraph 10 in the part that pertains to May 1996, and I would particularly like to say that there is Document 2D 00492 and 2D 00493. These are tables that refer to the resources used for taking care of refugees and expellees from 1992 until 1997. All this information was provided by the government of the Republic of Croatia, the office for displaced persons and refugees. I'd like to ask you something else now. We saw some information here as to what was done and to what extent by Croatia?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Excuse me, Your Honour. Your Honour, there haven't been any questions put to the witness about these documents at all. I don't understand the procedure. I'm sorry, I've been doing this for quite some years now. You can't just simply go through a list of documents, read the numbers into the record, and not put a question to the witness. We've now gone quickly through about four or five documents. Not a single question has been put to the witness, nor has the witness confirmed any of these documents. And I'm just saying so there's no confusion on the point when it comes time for a motion to admit these exhibits the Prosecution is going to oppose it as there's been no foundation through this witness as to the -- as to any of these, virtually any of the documents, there may have been one or two exceptions at the beginning; I'll have to go back and look. But certainly in the last few minutes, there's been no validation, not even a question to the witness, about any of these documents.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, the Prosecutor has is the right to oppose this, and I imagine that that's what he will do. But I assume that he will first look at the transcript from the witness's testimony. The witness confirmed that she knew about this information and these tables only contained this information structured in a particular way. I'm not going to put any special questions to this witness. This witness was asked considerably about what she knew and what she remembered, and she said what she knew and she said what she didn't know and what she remembered, what she didn't remember. There's quite a bit of information. I just don't want to go through all these statistics any long are, because I don't have enough time but these are statistics that pertain to the analysis that was read out.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Excuse me, Your Honour, I won't belabour it much longer, but just to make the point. We just went over, for example, we've lasted on the page, but I believe 2900488 if I'm not mistaken. And again Your Honour, there wasn't a single question. The witness hasn't verified a single document on this page and for counsel to say, she says she's seen some material before; she's seen some official documents somewhere before, in general, adds nothing. I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Nozica, you've submitted and shown a number of tables. Let me take, for example, the table in Exhibit 492. We see a number of tables, a number of figures, but put questions to the witness to support your case. Tell the witness listen here, We have a table with these figures. Witness, can you tell me and so on and so forth, and then the witness might or might not agree with you, because if you're just trying to say that the Croatian government spent a lot of money, yes, we can see that. It's obvious. But we're not going to spend hours on that. We can see that a lot of money has been spent and this has not been challenged. The witness therefore might confirm or not what you're saying and then you can move on to something else.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, that was precisely the aim of everything I was doing that it would become evident to you that Croatia spent a lot of money. I could have done it through this analysis and as for the tables, it is unnecessary for me to show the witness each and every one of them. I will do that if I'm given extra time. But I said for the transcript that, for example, table 2D 00494, I am kindly asking you whether we can look at this document on e-court. D 00494. Does it to correspond to information from paragraph 10 of the report -- of the report that is under number 2D 00496? You can compare. So it corresponds to this information -- may I just finish please, Mr. Prosecutor. It has to do with April 1995. If you allow me to finish, I will say that we see from these tables that are here that at the end of the table a figure is mentioned, 185.428. That is the total number of refugees in April 1995, in table -- in this table, rather, like in the analysis for April 1995.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, but what is your question for the witness?

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I have put a question to the witness, and the witness said in response that she knew some of these figures and did not know about others. These tables only contain statistics about the matters referred to in the analysis.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sorry, may I just --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: No, sorry, Witness, before --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Scott.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I'm not getting a microphone for some reason or another. Your Honour, we're about to lose it from the screen, but I think the answer we got sets it out quite well. On page 65, line 13 or 14, that we are about to lose, we saw, in fact, what the real motivation is. That was precisely the aim of everything that I was doing, Your Honour, and that would become evident to you that Croatia spent a lot of money. In other words, counsel was acting as a witness in presenting documents to the Chamber without putting any questions to the witness. The point of the exercise was for counsel to give what evidence to the Court and testify in place of the witness, and it was, indeed, simply to take the Chamber through documents for the purposes of the Chamber seeing documents, for which there is no evidence on the record at this point. And it would not be, with all due respect, I mean, this is a point of view, that's exactly the point. There is no evidence before the Chamber on this matter that has been confirmed by a witness, except Counsel's presentation. So I do object, Your Honour. This is not the proper way to proceed. And just now, Mr. President, when you cautioned counsel on putting the question to the witness, the only response was, and it's the only response we've received for the last 15 or 20 minutes, is the witness has said she saw -- she had seen some of these figures. Well, out of about ten documents so far, which of the figures had she seen and what does she know and what can she say about them?

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Your Honour, I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Murphy, I'll give you the floor later. But if the Defence wants to highlight that the Croatian government has spent money for the refugees, the way I would have gone about it would be as follows: I would ask the question to the witness. I would ask her whether she knew that the Croatian government had spent money. She would have said yes. Then you would proceed as follows: I'm going to submit a document related to money spent throughout the years 1993, 1994, et cetera. Can you confirm that these expenses correspond to the money spent by the Croatian government; and then the witness would say I can, I can't, et cetera. And thus we would save a lot of time. One day I should make a demonstration for you to get you to understand how you should go about it. Ms. Nozica, please put questions to the witness, questions that are useful for the Chamber to try and highlight what you want to establish. You're trying to establish that the Croatian government has spent money. Okay. But that you can do extremely quickly. You just ask the witness whether she was aware of it. If she was not aware of it, then you can ask how come at the embassy she had no information about the budget, et cetera, and then you can start a line of questioning.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Your Honour. I would like to be heard briefly on this, because I think it does raise a couple important points of principle. Firstly, what Ms. Nozica has been doing with this witness is exactly what we have spent month after month after month listening to Mr. Scott do with witnesses, asking -- putting documents to them and asking them whether that corresponds with their knowledge and experience. May I finish, Mr. Scott, please? The record will be quite clear when Your Honours look at it, as I was, following it line by line, that that is what my colleague was doing. And what we've been presented with here, Your Honour, is documents which are clearly come from a very reliable source. I know it's inconvenient for the Prosecution to be confronted with facts very often in this case, but that's what's happening here. And Mr. Scott is entitled, afterwards, wards to make whatever objections he wants to the exhibits. We will make a response. One of the things we can say in our response is that we have been inundated over the last few days with requests for admissions of evidence by the Prosecution for documents of a very similar nature emanating from public authorities, which Mr. Scott blandly says are admissible under 89(C). Now, he can have it one way or the other, but not both ways. If the Prosecution can adduce official documents and put them in evidence, we can do the same, whether or not the witness testifies about their contents. These are documents that come from the Republic of Croatia. And, Your Honour, we'll make that argument in it due course, but what Ms. Nozica did was to very properly put questions to this witness to ask whether certain figures corresponded with -- with her knowledge. The witness in some cases said it did; in some cases said it didn't. Now, if Mr. Scott had been listening to the testimony, he would have understood that the other documents Ms. Nozica referred to are, in fact, tables, which present in summary form the more detailed information presented in the -- in the report; and to save time, Ms. Nozica referred to them for the purpose of the record. That's all that happened. Mr. Scott's intervention was completely inappropriate, and he can make his objections at a later time. And I ask that Ms. Nozica to now be allowed to continue with her cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I think, Mr. Murphy, I think it is necessary to recall that according to the rules established by this Chamber and practice, during the presentation of the Prosecution's evidence, the Prosecution can introduce documents which have not been put to a witness because they could not, you know, you're quite aware. The Defence will have that possibility when the Defence presents its case, but not now. These are the rules we have established. So your comparison, with due respect, is not entirely fair.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Well, if that's the -- if that's the case, Your Honour, I -- I will have to go back to the Court's previous rulings and look at the orders that were made. If that's true, I'm very surprised to hear that. It's not my recollection -- it's not my recollection. I'm not saying Your Honour is wrong. I'll have to look at it, of course, and maybe Your Honour has the order in front of him and -- and will be able to correct me. But, Your Honour, it -- what we're doing here, Your Honour, and we've been doing throughout this trial is to introduce in cross-examination documents tendered by the Defence. I think that's happened on a consistent basis. There have been numerous orders by the Trial Chamber admitting such documents tendered by the Defence on exactly the basis we're doing now. And, Your Honour, I see no basis for Your Honours to say that we may not use public documents from the Republic of Croatia in order to cross-examine a witness, who was in an official position with the embassy in Zagreb at the material time. It's the only way to confront her with the facts. I know that's inconvenient for the Prosecution, but I think it's a legitimate function of cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Murphy, there may be a misunderstanding here. The documents submitted by the Defence will, of course, be admitted by the Defence if the documents are -- have a probative value and are relevant, especially since these documents have been provided as part of the cooperation with the Tribunal. This document was provided on the 12th of June, 1998, to the OTP as part of the cooperation with the OTP. What matters for the Judges is the substance of these documents and what you want to highlight in these documents. That's what I wanted to draw your attention upon, because obviously the witness was not familiar with these documents. She can't talk about the figures. The only thing she can say is of a very general nature. In other words, did the Croatian government budget certain expenses for the refugees? She said yes, and then we move on to something else. But spending so much time reading out figures in tables, it's waste of time. A waste of time for you, a waste of time for me. I'd rather we moved ahead. Of course, these tables are extremely interesting, especially when I see that there is a breakdown of refugees according to the various localities. Mr. Scott, you wanted to take the floor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: May I just answer Mr. Murphy. I would refer you to the decision of 13 July 2006. It's number 6, which says that under the conditions hereafter, the Prosecutor can, after hearing of a witness, and so forth, and this is not -- this does not refer to both parts. We have discussed this in Chambers, actually. So that is the reference of what I referred to.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, obviously, I don't have the advantage of knowing what Your Honours discussed in Chambers. In order to save time, may I just say, Your Honour, of course, and I take Judge Antonetti's point that we -- we need to -- there are certain times when, of course, we need to move on. It is, if I may say so, however, just another illustration of the problems at that arise because we don't have sufficient time. If there were time to go through these documents line by line, we do -- we could, of course, do what Mr. Scott apparently wants us to do, but, Your Honour, we have to do what we can given the time. And if we're going to stand on -- on formalities here and say, well, we can't consider these documents now, and at some later time they're going to come in, then a great deal of time will be wasted. And we won't have the opportunity of challenging this witness on very important points. Your Honour, despite the order of the 13th of July, I would respectfully submit that if information is tendered by the Defence that that challenges the substance of a witness's evidence, that is information that the Trial Chamber should consider. It may be that -- that later the statistics may have to be proved in their own right, but it would be a disadvantage to the Chamber if you can't have a witness confronted with facts relating to her testimony. That's all we're trying to do, and it shifts the burden of proof away from the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. Scott.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I hope the Chamber appreciates my patience. It's very difficult when one stands up not to -- not to be tempted to try to respond to everything that's been said in the last few minutes, but I won't attempt that. I leave it to the Chamber's good judgement and recall of the record itself as to what's been said and not said. My only points -- I only have two points to make very briefly. One is I would invite counsel not to personalise these comments and talk about, you know, what the Prosecution is afraid of and not to be confronted. It's inconvenient to be confronted with the facts. When I stand up and made my objection, I was not personal to the counsel on other side. I simply made a legal objection. I didn't make personal comments about her or any other counsel. I don't think it adds anything, frankly. Number one. And I would just ask, and I would ask and invite my colleagues, that is not necessary to engage in that sort of behaviour. Number two, Your Honour, more importantly, my only point is this: Of course, both parties can put in documents from public sources at the appropriate time. I don't want to be inconsistent. Absolutely, I think there are documents that should come in on their own, and the Chamber has provided -- the Chamber has provided vehicles for doing that. What I do object to and what I don't think is proper cross-examination -- excuse me, Your Honour. No. I'm not finished, but I'm just waiting to have the Chamber's attention. What is not proper, Your Honour, and my only point is, my only point is that this is cross-examination and we have a witness on the stand, and there shouldn't be any pretense that the witness has added anything to the material that's been put in front of her. That's the point. Not whether these documents can be tendered in some other way. They probably can. And, indeed, the Prosecution will use various vehicles available to it under the Rules to tender documents, but that is not the same thing to sit here in court and go quickly go through a bunch of documents, as if, as if the witness is adding value to them. That is the problem and that's the nature of my objection. But, Mr. President, as you said some minutes ago, if that's how the hour of cross-examination wants to be spent, then I suppose it's up to them to use the time or waste the time as they see fit.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Your Honour, I apologise --

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: -- if I personalised anything regarding Mr. Scott. I inadvertently borrowed some language he used in response to Mr. Karnavas yesterday, which I probably shouldn't have done.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank. Ms Alaburic.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, you say something, and hopefully remind all present in this courtroom, of something that Judge Trechsel said in July 2006 about the possibility of admitting evidence into the record. If you remember when this decision was passed, the Defence counsel reacted straight away to the fact that the Prosecutor has the right to tender some documents irrespective of witnesses. And we said immediately that we thought that this infringed upon the equality of arms in the proceedings involved, and we were given an explanation to the effect that, of course, this right does not only pertain to the Prosecution but that equal rights are enjoyed by the Defence too. We trusted that interpretation, and we did not ask for the decision to be changed in writing as well. If that would be the interpretation of the entire Trial Chamber, what His Honour Judge Trechsel said just now, we will certainly initiate an amendment of this decision. Otherwise, we, Defence counsel and our clients, will not be in a position to fully avail ourselves of the right to defence during the Prosecution case. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Nozica, we might have wasted 20 minutes, and I would have rather taken a look at your documents so please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. I hope this isn't my 20 minutes, but I just wish to explain one point. I showed an official document by the government of Croatia which shows and I'm sorry to say this in front of the witness there is no need for her to go out. What the Croatian state did not only in terms of money and Your Honour asked the witness to see how much money was spent. I never expected the witness to know that. She was in the embassy of another state. But I had to go through each of these facts and figures to test whether the witness knows about it, and she did confirm knowing about some of those elements. So this document speaks of the overall efforts made by Croatia during a time which in the indictment comes under joint criminal enterprise. Now, for me every confirmation by this witness for even the smallest statistical figure is sufficient for the time being. There will be more witnesses coming in, Mr. Praljak will be doing the work for me, there will be other evidence that we're going to present, but for the transcript I'd like to make this clear. The Prosecutor today did precisely something that you reprimanded the Defence for yesterday. He came across a document which does not correspond to -- which doesn't suit the Prosecutor. It was an official document so he intentionally interrupted us. It showed things that were notoriously well-known. And if -- unless we deal with these documents in the courtroom, he will have the opportunity of lodging a complaint in due course to object. So if he considers that some of these tables were not treated with the witness, let him raise an objection, but please may I be allowed to conduct my cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please proceed then.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Madam, just to finish off this topic about money and funds. I understood you to say that you didn't have this information, you didn't know how much money Croatia spent and if you ever saw the facts and figures you don't remember them. Would that be the correct interpretation of what you wanted to say?

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Thank you. Now I have in front of me a document, and I assume you have the Prosecution binder in front of you still. Just to make a brief comparison. The document is P 04150 [Realtime transcript read in error "P 0415"]. It's a Prosecution document, Prosecution binder. The number again P, Prosecution, 0415. And you'll tell me when you've found it. You signed it. It is a report on the problems of RBH in the State of Croatia. Have you found the document?

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: It is dated the 13th of August, 1993, and I'm going to refer to page 2 of the Croatian version, and that will be found on ERN number 0218. 8.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Just a point on the record. You have said P 0415. It is P 04150, and it was wrong in the record. So that could have misled.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, thank you. That is indeed the document. So for Their Honours, I'm going to say that the ERN number is as follows 02188966.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: And in the Croatian version, madam, it is on page 2. And it is the last paragraph in the Croatian text, and it is the second paragraph on the page that I quoted in English. Now, today we spoke about refugees in other countries, but if we compare, and that's what I'd like to do now since this is your own observation, where it says that Turkey would take in 2.000 of our citizens in two collective centres, put up towards the Bulgarian border, one 100 kilometres and the other 130 kilometres away from Istanbul. And it says here that there are 2.000 refugees there already. Now, this is the portion that I'd like to focus on about the use of funds and resources. It says: "Turkey would be ready to meet the costs of transport from Croatia from an earlier given amount of money of 40 million US dollars." That's the information you received, that Turkey was ready to take in these additional 2.000 refugees, but the Bosnians should pay for their own transport to Turkey?

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was writing about what Ambassador Tufan informed me about.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: My colleague Mr. Karnavas asked you about the status and conditions of certain refugees. Now, can you make a comparison between what Croatia did and the situation facing refugees in Denmark? And you and I, as BH citizens, know about all this. We spent many -- a lot of time on ships and ferries. Can you give me a general assessment? You don't know how much money Croatia spent, you say. However, on the basis of the conditions under which refugees lived in other countries and the conditions -- compared to the conditions they lived in in Croatia, can you give us your assessment, a general assessment of how much Croatia did for the Bosnian refugees?

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry, but I can't.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Can you tell us then whether most of the Bosnian refugees were put up in Croatia along the coast, or, rather, most of these people were put up along the Adriatic coast?

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know whether most of them, but that a large number of them were, that I can confirm.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Was there a large number of refugees arriving in 1992 put up in the holiday centres and hotels and given collective accommodation there; is that right?

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is right. I can confirm that.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Right. Now, in Turkey, did Turkey offer accommodation to refugees along the borders -- its borders with Bulgaria not as in Untily [phoen] but just like -- but, whereas, Croatia offered them accommodation along the Adriatic coast?

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is correct that Turkey offered what I stipulate in the letter.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Well, would that mean that conditions were better? And we must not forget that Croatia itself was at war and some of its territory in the north was occupied and that the refugees were accommodated far away from the crisis zones? So just on that point would you say that Croatia offered the refugees from Bosnia-Herzegovina much better conditions than did most of the European countries? Can you confirm that?

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I could not.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: All right. I don't want to insist. Can you tell me then how much the state of Bosnia and Herzegovina spent on refugees in Croatia through the department and office that you worked for?

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I'm sorry, I can't say that. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Why can't you tell me that? Why can't you say? Do you not know or what?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PRANDLER
utterances.text: I'm sorry to interrupt you. Of course I'm not here for speaking about the situation and the conditions, let's say, in those camps when we had in Hungary during the war, but I may say that it is rather difficult to compare the situation and the conditions in different countries. Of course, Hungary didn't have the Adriatic Coast, itself, a very nice place to be. On the other hand, I believe that the conditions should be and could be determined, not only by the geographic situation of a camp but really what is being offered to the refugees. And since I happened to be there in the camps in Baranja, in southern part of Hungary, of course, in this case we try to do our best, I mean, the Hungarian government, to help. I'm just saying this because you asked the question if the situation, overall situation, and the conditions were better in Croatia than in, let's say, Turkey, or some other countries. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm -- I'm grateful for that intervention. I just ask my colleague for permission to make a short observation which would be, of course -- I'm sure Your Honour would be aware of the importance of not bringing any personal knowledge that he may have from his own observation as a substitute for the evidence given by the witnesses in this case. I know Your Honour appreciates the importance of that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PRANDLER
utterances.text: Yes, I accept this. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I did not wish to make any comparisons between individual countries, but I did take the example of Turkey. And I say here that Turkey agreed to -- to take in 2.000 of our citizens, but they are requiring funds to transport them from Croatia to Turkey. I think the witness knows quite a bit about this, and I wanted to obtain an evaluation from the witness about the accommodation of the refugees in Croatia, but she said she wouldn't comment. So I now went on and asked what Bosnia and Herzegovina as state spent in Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Madam, how big was your budget in the embassy for the refugees from Bosnia-Hercegovina? I assume you had a budget of some kind?

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Budget, you mean the funds of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina? I don't know which budget you mean.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: I mean your department in Zagreb at the embassy. Did you receive funds, resources which allowed to you act and intervene when it came to refugees?

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: In cooperation with the NGO sectors and UN organisations, we did dispose of certain funds based on projects financed by donators, by donors. And I can't tell you that now, because I can't speak of any total sum or the specific project -- project involved.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: But I didn't ask you that. I asked you about the funds, the resources, money. Just a moment, please for the transcript. I was speaking about funds given to you by the Bosnia-Herzegovina government to be used on refugees, Bosnian refugees, in Croatia, so funds from the budget of the State of Bosnia-Herzegovina or other funds for that matter, of Bosnia-Herzegovina. I'm not referring to donations, and I'm not referring to the monies collected from non-governmental organisations. My first question is what the BH government gave to be spent on refugees.

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: During my mandate, the directorate for displaced persons and refugees provided 50.000 marks for the requirements of the teaching staff in extra territorial schools of the BH in the RC. I assume that this was from the BH budget, funds from the budget, but I can't claim that. But those funds came from the directorate to the department.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: And do you know whether the embassy came by funds in different ways? Do you know about the logistical centres, military logistical centres were financed, for example, logistical centres of the state of BH in Croatia? Do you know about that?

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: I'm now going to look at -- ask you to look at 2D 00 - and it will be the last document before the break - 497. 2D 00497 is the document number. I think it's the third document from the bottom. Tell me when you've found it.

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have got the document.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: It is an article entitled, "The Secret of the Suitcase with a Million Dollars." You have the text in Croatia. So leaf through three or four pages and you'll see that you have the document there. It is the independent weekly called "Dani."

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: May we have it on e-court? The page number is 2D 380170. It is the 184th issue of Dan, and the text is identical.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: And I'm going to it read something out to you which relates to the financing and money that possibly the embassy might have had at its disposal, even for refugees. It says here, "The secret suitcase with a million dollars." It has who the member of the Bosnian government is. "Dr. Fatih Ali Hassanien, director and founder of the TWRA, every week handed over a suitcase with a million American dollars, which he -- was sent by the Islamic world to the Bosnians." I'll ask my question at the end. It says, "The embassies, the BH Embassy in Zagreb and Vienna, are the key to understanding Bosniak war diplomacy, which is at the foundations of today's diplomatic representation of Bosnia-Herzegovina. They were two of the most murky and linked-up embassies for only one reason. Both of them functioned in close connection with the TWRA, and the circle around Dr. Fatih Ali Hassanien says a Bosniak investigator of war crimes who during 1993 and 1994 was in contact with most of the RBiH embassies in western Europe." I'm going to skip the next paragraph. Now, the editorial offices of the weekly Dan, for the record. It was a weekly published in Bosnia-Herzegovina in Sarajevo, was it not?

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is a weekly that is published in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: "The editorial offices of Dan," it says, "are in possession of original documents which show the impotence of official organs to uncover parallel influences, links, and the course followed by money in Bosnian diplomatic circles in Vienna and Zagreb." And then there is mention of an investigation conducted against TWRA, and I'm going to read the penultimate paragraph on the first page. It says, "The money which arrived mostly from Saudi Arabia, Brunei, and Pakistan did not reach Ali Hassanien, only on the basis of the seven bank accounts." Seven bank accounts are mentioned in the previous paragraph, but in the suitcase as well?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I apologise for interrupting. But before it's about to leave the screen now, on line 21 of page 81 attributes some text as an answer of the witness, when it was not an answer of the witness. We've lost it now, I'm afraid, but perhaps someone can go back in e-court. But there was an indication on that line that some text was the answer of the witness and it was not. It was the continuing part of the question. In fact, there hasn't been an answer. The witness hasn't given an answer, except to identify a weekly publication in Sarajevo for some minutes. So while I'm on my feet, Your Honour, as of now - there may be questions coming - but as of now, we're back to simply reading documents to the court, which the Chamber may find interesting, but I note without putting any questions to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I do ask you, and I said this at the beginning. Well, I have to ask the witness something. I wasn't able to prepare the witness, who showed her -- who was shown a series of documents by the Prosecution. So I'm showing this, and it is only proper that the Trial Chamber and the witness sees these documents and knows what they're about.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: So, madam, I'll just say, very briefly. It says, "The money arrived in suitcases at the beginning the war. Dr. Fatih travelled from Vienna to Zagreb on a weekly basis by car with a suitcase full of money, Sudanese number plates, and there were 3 to 5 million American dollars in the suitcase. On a regular basis Dr. Hassanein, with respect to an investigation carried out by the Austrian and German police, claimed that he handed over the money in Zagreb to a member of the Bosnian government." Now, madam, I'm just going to ask you something in that regard, very short questions. Did you know about the writings of this weekly? I'm sure you read it in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean about the press writings?

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Yes. Did you know that an investigation was conducted into the alleged money. I say alleged, but about the money that reached Zagreb in a suitcase?

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Just from these sources, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: And, in that respect, did you give out any information?

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Did you have any knowledge to the effect that money came to the embassy in some ways that would have been apart from the budget of Bosnia-Herzegovina, apart from NGO resources?

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Did you ever ask authorised officials, the ambassador or anyone else in the embassy, to allocate certain funds for the hardest hit categories of refugees that addressed you?

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: The information I had was that there were no resource, and that's why I did not make such requests.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: If necessary, we can take the break now; and then after the break, I'm going to calculate how much time I have left, and then I'm will continue my cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We are going to break for 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think Mr. Scott would like to speak.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I'm reluctant to take courtroom time, but I know we won't finish with the witness today under any scenario. And I'm afraid if I wait until 1.45, I know everyone tends to try to move out the courtroom rather quickly. So two quick matters, Your Honour. When I make -- when the Prosecution, and I'm sure the Defence as well, makes a commitment to the Chamber to provide certain information, we want to follow through on that. And, yesterday, Judge Trechsel raised a question about a handwritten notation, a number on one of the documents. It was document Exhibit P 10060. And in the transcript, yesterday, Judge Trechsel raised a question of why on the English translation there was -- the number 104425 had been put on the translation as indicating it was handwritten on the original. I have may have had the inquiry, Your Honours, and my initial explanation was -- was in fact wrong, but what I did find was that it was -- it's simply a number that apparently was put on by CLSS, the interpreters, for their own administrative purposes. It was not on the original document as it came into the Tribunal, but CLSS has a certain numbering system sometimes, and it was a number that they added, and then whoever did the English translation carried it over on. So, Your Honour, that's the information on that point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Secondly, Your Honours, and I'm going to say this because the witness is here and I don't want to take the time to excuse here. But if I can address the matter without mentioning any particular name, and I'll hopefully everyone in the courtroom will be cautious in this regard. The Prosecution is due to make a certain filing today that was discussed earlier. We are asking to be granted some additional -- some additional words, and again without describing exactly what the pleadings are. The Defence to date on this same matter have filed a total of 30 pages worth of pleadings comprising some 9.926 words, 9.926 words. The Prosecution to date has filed seven pages and 2.601 words. The Chamber previously grand us leave to file a reply, and we're asking to be able to file a reply somewhere in the vicinity of about 4.800 words, which will still bring us well under the total words used by the Defence if the Chamber agrees.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You are granted the permission to do so. You are allowed up to 4.800 words.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Fine. Well, we still have 45 minutes; and according to the time imparted to the Defence, it is time granted to Ms. Nozica. So, Ms. Nozica, you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Ms. Krajsek, I'm going to ask you to look at a document, 2D 0009. That is the first document in my binder, as far as I can see.

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have the document.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: We have very little time. Could you look at least at the first page. Do you know this document? It was compiled on the 16th of July when you were in the Embassy of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina in Zagreb.

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not familiar with this document.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: All right. I'm going to ask you about some of the persons mentioned in this document and you probably know them. So this is a document of the embassy of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina in Zagreb, and it gives the names of certain persons who live in the -- who work in the military economic office and in the logistics department of the Supreme Command Staff or, rather, they initiate proceedings for the official appointment of these persons. Please look at these persons. Do you know any of the six persons mentioned here in the military economic office, and can you confirm whether you came across them when you were in Zagreb?

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Except for the person under number 3 -- rather, number 6, Blanka Vucak. I saw all the rest of them while I was in Zagreb.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: For the interpreters, I have to caution both of us, myself and you. After my question, we should make a small break, a pause, you and I, so that we do not overlap.

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Can I just ask that they let me hear the interpreter because then I will realise how long they take to finish. It will be easier.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: You can hear the interpreters from a distance and you can also look at the transcript in front of you, and you can follow that. Tell me -- this other logistics department of the Supreme Command Staff of the Armed Forces of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina in Zagreb, there is 21 names mentioned here. Can you tell us whether you came across any of these persons in Zagreb and whether you were in touch with them in any way?

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I met persons 2, 3, 4. I'm not sure, but number 14 sounds familiar. Those are the only persons that I came across, and I only had contacts with them that would boil down to saying hello to each other, but I didn't have any official contact.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Thank you. We see here that this has to do with the procedure of legalising these centres dated the 16th of July, 1993. Did you have any knowledge to the effect that these persons had been in Zagreb before this date as well?

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: As for Mr. Hasan Cengic, did you see him in Zagreb in the embassy or somewhere else?

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did, but outside the period when I was engaged as the attache for refugees.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Could you please tell me then what this period was then?

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: 1992. September and October, because then I was waiting in Zagreb for humanitarian flights that would enable me to return to my country. That's when I met him.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: So I can conclude that you were a rather frequent guest at the embassy in 1992 as well. You did not have an official capacity, but you came there to see how you could get to Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was no embassy at the time. There was the office of the BH in the Republic of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: And that's when you saw Mr. Hasan Cengic as you said. Did you come across any other people from this list?

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Possibly. But, you know, perhaps I didn't know their names. I did not know of having seen them.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Did you know that there were logistics departments of the Supreme Command of the armed forces of BH in Zagreb?

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Within the embassy did you have any staff meetings these different departments? Did you know about who was doing what?

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not have any comprehensive information about this in terms of what the tasks and duties were of certain individuals. We had a few staff meetings and the plan was to have regular meetings, at least once a week, but after one or two meetings this practice withered away.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Could we now look at 2D 00498. That is the one but last document in my binder. Just tell me when you find it.

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have the document.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: I would like to say for the transcript that this is a document that was provided by the Prosecutor to us according to Rule 68. It is a rather comprehensive document, probably related to the TVRA agency. At least that is what I infer, but can you just help me with part of this document, and that part is even translated. Please, could we just look at the first page of this document. We have a few pictures here, a few photographs, some of which have dates as well. I would just like to ask you, because your copy is far more legible than what it is in e-court. Please look at these photographs and tell me whether you can recognise any of these people. I have to tell you that according to my knowledge this document was obtained from the Bosnian embassy that was in Zagreb.
